newsitem.title: USA: Treasury begins selling new security next week.
newsitem.headline: Treasury begins selling new security next week.

text.p: The Treasury will hold its first auction next Wednesday of a new, inflation-protected security that Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin said could spawn major changes in financial markets.

The Treasury will sell $7 billion of a new class of 10-year notes designed to offer protection against having their principal, or face value, eroded by rising prices as happens all too often with traditional borrowing instruments like bonds.

Sold in denominations as low as $1,000, they will pay interest twice a year. The interest rate set at auction will be fixed but the principal will be adjusted for the impact of inflation and the semiannual interest payments will be based on the adjusted principal.

The Treasury will use changes in the Consumer Price Index for urban consumers, a basket of price changes that is published monthly by the government and widely used as a gauge of inflation, to calculate adjustments in the securities' principal value.

Rubin predicted the new securities will be attractive for everyone from middle-class savers putting money away for their childrens' education to big institutional investors seeking another product to sell.

"For the first time, the United States is offering investors protection from inflation," Rubin said at a news conference, finally bringing to fruition an idea that he said has been kicked around at the Treasury since the 1940s.
Rubin, a long-time Wall Street trader before he became Treasury Secretary, said the potential ramifications from the new security were wide-ranging.
"We believe that over time it may well spawn significant changes in the financial markets," he said.

"It could encourage investors to think about investments more in terms of real rates of return, which in turn could lead intermediaries like mutual funds to offer 'purchasing power' products such as indexed annuities," he suggested.

The Treasury plans to sell inflation-indexed securities four times a year. Other maturities besides a 10-year note will be added but no decision has yet been taken on how soon or whether it will be for a shorter or longer term than 10 years, Rubin said.
Rubin stressed that the Treasury, though it borrows billions of dollars weekly through debt auctions, was very conservative about introducing new products like inflation-proetcted securtities.
"This is a big idea, and now it is a reality," he said. "It has the potential to increase the rate of savings and it will in time also enable the Treasury to borrow at a lower cost of money."
